questions.stem: A 39 year old man with polycystic kidney disease has a sudden, severe headache while lifting a heavy box. He says it was the worst pain of his life and peaked within seconds. He has vomited three times. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 64 bpm, BP 172/98 mmHg and GCS 15. He has neck stiffness and is photophobic.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A thunderclap headache with meningism in a patient with polycystic kidney disease (associated with berry aneurysms) is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise.

clues: worst pain of his life and peaked within seconds
steps.x: Thunderclap headache, meningism and a known association.

elim: Develops over hours with fever, not a headache peaking within seconds.
Unilateral orbital pain with autonomic features, recurring in bouts.
Gradual headache with confusion and very high BP, without sudden onset.
Builds over minutes to hours, not instantly 'the worst ever'.

steps.x: E: Subarachnoid haemorrhage. Thunderclap headache + PKD = subarachnoid haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman collapses at a family barbecue. Her husband says she grabbed the back of her head, vomited and then had a generalised seizure lasting 2 minutes. Her sister died of a brain haemorrhage aged 50. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm, BP 184/102 mmHg and GCS 12.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden headache, vomiting, collapse, seizure and reduced consciousness, with smoking and a family history of SAH, point to subarachnoid haemorrhage.

clues: grabbed the back of her head
sister died of a brain haemorrhage
steps.x: Sudden occipital headache then seizure and reduced GCS, with family history.

elim: The seizure followed a sudden headache and vomiting, suggesting a structural bleed.
Would not cause sudden occipital headache.
Does not cause collapse, seizures and a GCS of 12.
Recovery is rapid and complete without seizure or reduced GCS.

steps.x: D: Subarachnoid haemorrhage. Family history and smoking are risk factors; SAH can present with collapse and seizures.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has a sudden, severe headache and vomiting that began 4 hours ago. She is drowsy with a GCS of 13 and has neck stiffness. Her pulse rate is 62 bpm and BP 176/96 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows blood in the subarachnoid space. The admitting doctor performs fundoscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on fundoscopy?
o: Cherry red spot at the macula
Cotton wool spots and hard exudates
questions.e: Retinal (subhyaloid) haemorrhages from the sudden rise in ICP are a recognised examination finding in subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: Confirmed SAH; what is seen in the eye?

elim: Central retinal artery occlusion.
Signs of chronic hypertensive or diabetic retinopathy.
Age-related macular degeneration.
Takes weeks to develop after optic nerve damage.

steps.x: E: Retinal haemorrhages. SAH examination: neck stiffness, reduced GCS, focal signs, retinal haemorrhages.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has a headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. He has nausea and vomited once. Brudzinski's sign is positive. There is no rash. The doctor is trying to decide between bacterial meningitis and subarachnoid haemorrhage.
questions.q: Which additional feature would most strongly suggest subarachnoid haemorrhage?
o: Headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute
questions.e: Meningism, photophobia, vomiting and even a mild fever occur in both; the onset is the key: a thunderclap headache peaking within a minute means SAH.

steps.x: Meningism with a low-grade fever, which both conditions cause.

elim: Mild fever occurs in both.
Occur in both.
A feature of meningism in both.
A meningeal sign, present in both.

steps.x: A: Headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute. The thunderclap onset separates SAH from meningitis.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man is recovering on the neurosurgical ward after coiling of a ruptured berry aneurysm. He has had hypertension since his twenties. His father needed dialysis from the age of 50. Abdominal examination shows bilateral ballotable masses in both flanks. His BP is 168/100 mmHg. Urinalysis shows blood ++.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.e: Bilateral flank masses, early hypertension, haematuria and a parent on dialysis indicate ADPKD (PKD1, chromosome 16), a recognised association of berry aneurysm and SAH.

clues: bilateral ballotable masses in both flanks
steps.x: Family history of renal failure, early hypertension and bilateral flank masses.

elim: Associated with berry aneurysms and hypertension but not flank masses or familial renal failure.
Associated with aneurysms but with skin and joint hypermobility, not flank masses.
Tall stature and aortic root disease, not bilateral flank masses.
Usually a unilateral mass, not a familial bilateral pattern.

steps.x: A: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Berry aneurysm + bilateral flank masses = ADPKD.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman has a sudden severe headache and collapses. CT head shows blood in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 180/100 mmHg. She has no history of trauma. Her son asks where the vessel that bled is most likely to be.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the bleeding vessel?
o: A berry aneurysm at the Circle of Willis
Bridging veins between cortex and dural sinuses
questions.e: Spontaneous SAH is most commonly from a ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm at an arterial bifurcation of the Circle of Willis.

clues: blood in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures
steps.x: Spontaneous subarachnoid blood at the base of the brain.

elim: These bleed in subdural haemorrhage.
Cause deep hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage.
Bleeds in extradural haemorrhage after trauma.
Dissection here causes posterior circulation stroke and neck pain.

steps.x: A: A berry aneurysm at the Circle of Willis. Spontaneous SAH = ruptured berry aneurysm, Circle of Willis.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man is admitted with a subarachnoid haemorrhage at 09:00. CT angiography shows an anterior communicating artery aneurysm and coiling is planned for the next morning. At 17:00 he complains of a sudden new severe headache and his GCS falls from 15 to 9. His BP is 196/104 mmHg. Repeat CT shows more subarachnoid blood than before.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
questions.e: A sudden new headache and drop in GCS within the first 12 hours, with more blood on CT, is an early rebleed of the unsecured aneurysm.

steps.x: Within 12 hours, unsecured aneurysm, more blood on CT.

elim: Occurs at 7 to 14 days, and would not increase subarachnoid blood.
Causes gradual drowsiness with enlarged ventricles, not a new thunderclap.
Would not increase blood on CT.
Causes gradual confusion over days with hyponatraemia.

steps.x: A: Aneurysmal rebleed. Early rebleed occurs within 12 hours; secure the aneurysm early.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman had a subarachnoid haemorrhage treated by endovascular coiling. She was alert with a GCS of 15 after the procedure. The ward team is told to watch closely for confusion, drowsiness or new focal weakness from narrowing of the cerebral arteries. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 140/82 mmHg.
questions.q: When is this complication most likely to occur?
questions.e: Delayed cerebral vasospasm typically peaks 7 to 14 days after the bleed and can cause secondary ischaemic stroke.

steps.x: The complication is delayed vasospasm.

elim: Too late; vasospasm happens in the first 2 weeks.
Vasospasm is a delayed process, not procedural.
The window for early rebleeding, not vasospasm.
Too early for vasospasm, which develops as blood breaks down.

steps.x: A: 7 to 14 days after the bleed. Vasospasm: days 7 to 14. Rebleed: first 12 hours.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is on day 1 after a subarachnoid haemorrhage from a coiled posterior communicating artery aneurysm. A nurse finds him with rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for 2 minutes, followed by drowsiness. He has bitten his tongue. Within 30 minutes he returns to his baseline GCS of 15. Repeat CT head shows no new blood and normal ventricles. His sodium is 139 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Seizures are a recognised complication of SAH; normal CT and sodium exclude rebleed, hydrocephalus and SIADH.

clues: rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for 2 minutes
no new blood and normal ventricles
steps.x: A generalised seizure with normal repeat imaging and sodium.

elim: CT shows no new blood and he returned to baseline.
The ventricles are normal.
His sodium is normal.
Does not cause 2 minutes of rhythmic jerking, tongue biting and drowsiness.

steps.x: D: Seizure secondary to subarachnoid haemorrhage. Seizures are a complication of SAH; check for rebleed, hydrocephalus and hyponatraemia.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman is on day 5 after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. She has a new headache, nausea and muscle cramps and is more drowsy. She appears euvolaemic. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. She is not on diuretics.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pattern of results?
o: High serum osmolality with dilute urine
High serum sodium with high urine output
Low serum osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine
Low serum sodium with high serum potassium
Low serum sodium with very low urine sodium
questions.e: SIADH is a common consequence of SAH: inappropriate ADH release causes dilutional hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine with high urine sodium in a euvolaemic patient.

steps.x: Hyponatraemic symptoms days after SAH in a euvolaemic patient.

elim: Diabetes insipidus.
Also diabetes insipidus.
Suggests adrenal insufficiency.
Suggests hypovolaemia or low intake, not SIADH.

steps.x: C: Low serum osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine. SAH + hyponatraemia = SIADH: low serum osmolality, concentrated urine.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman has a sudden severe headache followed by drooping of her left eyelid and double vision. Her left pupil is dilated and the left eye looks down and out. She has neck stiffness. Her pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 170/94 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows subarachnoid blood.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the aneurysm?
questions.e: A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil and SAH indicates an aneurysm of the ipsilateral posterior communicating artery compressing the oculomotor nerve; CT angiography confirms it.

steps.x: SAH with a left pupil-involving third nerve palsy.

elim: Usually presents without a third nerve palsy.
Can cause bilateral eye movement problems but a unilateral painful third nerve palsy points to PComm.
Causes contralateral weakness or aphasia rather than an isolated third nerve palsy.
Would compress the right third nerve.

steps.x: D: Left posterior communicating artery. SAH + painful CN III palsy = ipsilateral PComm aneurysm.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man is found collapsed at home by a neighbour. He is confused and cannot give a history. He smokes and has hypertension. His pulse rate is 56 bpm, BP 188/104 mmHg and GCS 11. He has neck stiffness but no focal weakness. Non-contrast CT head shows hyperdense material in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures, with no blood in the brain parenchyma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hyperdense material in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures is blood in the subarachnoid space.

clues: hyperdense material in the basal cisterns
no blood in the brain parenchyma
steps.x: Collapse, meningism and blood in the cisterns.

elim: A crescentic collection over the convexity.
CT would not show hyperdense blood in the cisterns.
A lens-shaped collection after trauma.
Blood is within the brain parenchyma, which is spared here.

steps.x: E: Subarachnoid haemorrhage. Blood in the basal cisterns on CT = SAH.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with a long history of migraine has a headache that started suddenly while she was on the toilet. She says it was like being hit with a hammer, unlike her usual migraines, and it reached full intensity at once. She has vomited. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm, BP 168/96 mmHg and GCS 15. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A thunderclap headache on straining, different from usual headaches, is SAH even with a normal examination; a history of migraine does not exclude it.

clues: started suddenly while she was on the toilet
steps.x: Sudden onset, maximal at once, different from her usual headaches.

elim: Recurrent unilateral orbital pain with tearing.
Builds gradually and she says this is unlike her usual migraines.
Subacute temporal headache with jaw claudication in older patients.
Mild, band-like and gradual.

steps.x: C: Subarachnoid haemorrhage. A new 'worst ever' thunderclap headache is SAH until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has a sudden severe headache and neck stiffness. CT head confirms a subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm. A medical student asks which layers the blood is lying between. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 162/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Between which layers is the blood most likely to be found?
o: Inner table of the skull and dura mater
questions.e: SAH is bleeding into the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and pia mater, which contains CSF.

steps.x: Name the space.

elim: The subdural space, where bleeding is from bridging veins.
The extradural space.
There is no space here; blood in the brain itself is intracerebral haemorrhage.
A subgaleal haematoma.

steps.x: A: Arachnoid mater and pia mater. Subarachnoid space = between arachnoid and pia, filled with CSF.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has a sudden, severe headache that began during a spin class 3 hours ago, with nausea and vomiting. She has taken no drugs. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 68 bpm, BP 164/92 mmHg and GCS 15. There is no rash and no limb weakness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: A thunderclap headache on exertion suggests SAH; blood irritates the meninges and causes neck stiffness and other meningeal signs.

steps.x: Exertional thunderclap headache: SAH.

elim: A pontine haemorrhage or opioid sign.
Meningococcal septicaemia; she has no rash.
Indicates functional leg weakness.
Parkinsonism.

steps.x: B: Neck stiffness. SAH examination: meningism (neck stiffness, Brudzinski), reduced GCS, focal signs.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man had a subarachnoid haemorrhage 8 days ago and his aneurysm was coiled on day 1. He has been taking oral nimodipine. Today he becomes confused and develops weakness of his right arm. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. CT head shows no new blood and normal ventricles.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his new symptoms?
questions.e: New focal deficit and confusion 7 to 14 days after SAH, with no new blood or hydrocephalus, is delayed vasospasm causing secondary ischaemia, triggered by blood breakdown products.

clues: no new blood and normal ventricles
steps.x: Day 8, focal deficit, CT excludes rebleed and hydrocephalus.

elim: The aneurysm is coiled and CT shows no new blood.
No fever, and the deficit is focal.
The ventricles are normal.
Causes global confusion with hyponatraemia, not focal arm weakness; his sodium is normal.

steps.x: C: Delayed cerebral vasospasm. Days 7 to 14 with new focal signs = vasospasm.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has a sudden severe headache that began at 14:00. Non-contrast CT head performed at 17:30 on a modern scanner is reported by a consultant radiologist as normal. She is alert with a GCS of 15 and no neck stiffness. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Do not perform lumbar puncture and consider an alternative diagnosis
Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset
questions.e: A normal CT within 6 hours of onset effectively excludes SAH, so lumbar puncture is not needed; look for another cause.

steps.x: CT was done 3.5 hours after onset and is normal.

elim: Not needed when SAH has been excluded.
Only needed if the CT is done more than 6 hours after onset.
Used for ischaemic stroke.
Adds nothing; CT within 6 hours is extremely sensitive.

steps.x: B: Do not perform lumbar puncture and consider an alternative diagnosis. Normal CT within 6 hours: no LP needed.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has a sudden occipital headache 90 minutes ago followed by vomiting. He has neck stiffness. His pulse rate is 60 bpm, BP 178/98 mmHg and GCS 14. An urgent non-contrast CT head is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the CT head?
o: Hyperdense material in the basal cisterns
Hypodense area in the MCA territory
Lens-shaped collection limited by suture lines
questions.e: Non-contrast CT within 6 hours is extremely sensitive for SAH and shows hyperdense blood in the subarachnoid space and basal cisterns.

steps.x: Classic SAH, scanned early.

elim: A subdural haemorrhage.
An established ischaemic infarct.
An extradural haemorrhage.
An abscess or tumour, and needs contrast.

steps.x: B: Hyperdense material in the basal cisterns. SAH on CT: hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man had a thunderclap headache 15 hours ago. CT head at 9 hours was normal and a lumbar puncture is performed now. The red cell count is similar in the first and last tubes.
questions.q: Which result most strongly supports a subarachnoid haemorrhage?
questions.e: At least 12 hours after onset, red cells in CSF break down to bilirubin, seen as xanthochromia and confirmed by spectrophotometry; this separates SAH from a traumatic tap.

clues: CT head at 9 hours was normal
similar in the first and last tubes
steps.x: LP done more than 12 hours after onset after a late normal CT.

elim: Normal and does not help.
Suggests viral meningitis.
Opening pressure in SAH is normal or raised.
Suggest multiple sclerosis.

steps.x: E: Raised CSF bilirubin on spectrophotometry. Raised CSF bilirubin (xanthochromia) confirms SAH.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman arrives at the emergency department 10 hours after a sudden severe headache during sex. She is alert with a GCS of 15 and has no neck stiffness. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. The registrar explains that a single test may not be enough to exclude a subarachnoid haemorrhage at this stage.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to confirm or exclude the diagnosis?
o: Non-contrast CT head, then lumbar puncture if normal
questions.e: The gold standard is CT head plus lumbar puncture: after 6 hours a normal CT must be followed by LP at least 12 hours after onset.

clues: 10 hours after a sudden severe headache
single test may not be enough
steps.x: Presenting after 6 hours.

elim: Finds aneurysms but does not exclude SAH, and many people have unruptured aneurysms.
CT must come first to look for blood and mass effect.
Used for ischaemic stroke.
After 6 hours a normal CT does not exclude SAH.

steps.x: E: Non-contrast CT head, then lumbar puncture if normal. Gold standard = CT head + LP (LP if CT normal after 6 hours).

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has a subarachnoid haemorrhage confirmed on non-contrast CT head. He is alert with a GCS of 14. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 158/90 mmHg. The neurosurgical team wants to identify the source of the bleeding and plan treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Once SAH is confirmed, CT angiography (sensitivity and specificity about 90%) identifies the underlying aneurysm, such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

clues: identify the source of the bleeding
steps.x: SAH is confirmed; now find the aneurysm.

elim: Assesses carotid stenosis, not intracranial aneurysms.
For seizures.
SAH is already confirmed; LP is for a normal CT after 6 hours.
Looks for a cardiac embolic source.

steps.x: B: CT angiography of the head. Find the cause of SAH with CT angiography.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has a sudden severe headache. She asks why the doctors are rushing to scan her immediately rather than waiting until the morning. Her GCS is 15, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. The consultant explains that the sensitivity of the non-contrast CT head for blood falls with time.
questions.q: Within what time of onset is a non-contrast CT head extremely sensitive for subarachnoid haemorrhage?
questions.e: Non-contrast CT is extremely sensitive within the first 6 hours; after that a normal CT needs lumbar puncture.

clues: sensitivity of the non-contrast CT head for blood falls with time
steps.x: The CT sensitivity window.

elim: The high-sensitivity window lasts longer than this.
This is the minimum time before LP, not the CT window.
CT sensitivity has fallen considerably by then.
This relates to starting nimodipine (72 to 96 hours), not imaging.

steps.x: D: 6 hours. CT sensitive within 6 hours; LP at least 12 hours.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man is on day 6 after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. He has become confused and nauseated. He is clinically euvolaemic and is not on diuretics. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg. His serum sodium has fallen from 139 to 124 mmol/L over 3 days. The team suspects SIADH.
questions.q: Which investigation would best support this diagnosis?
o: Paired serum and urine osmolality with urine sodium
questions.e: SIADH is shown by low serum osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urine sodium in a euvolaemic patient; it is caused by hypothalamic dysfunction after SAH.

steps.x: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia after SAH.

elim: Looks for the aneurysm, not the cause of hyponatraemia.
Not needed; SAH is already confirmed.
Does not distinguish SIADH.
Tests for adrenal insufficiency; useful later if SIADH tests are unclear, but not first.

steps.x: C: Paired serum and urine osmolality with urine sodium. Confirm SIADH with paired serum and urine osmolality and urine sodium.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman has a subarachnoid haemorrhage confirmed on CT in a district general hospital without neurosurgery. She has been assessed with an ABCDE approach and her airway is safe. Her GCS is 14, pulse rate 68 bpm and BP 166/92 mmHg. CT angiography shows a middle cerebral artery aneurysm.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Lumbar puncture to confirm the diagnosis
Urgent referral to the regional neurosurgical centre
questions.e: After ABCDE, SAH needs urgent neurosurgical referral to secure the aneurysm, with careful BP control if needed.

steps.x: Confirmed SAH in a hospital without neurosurgery.

elim: SAH is an emergency with a high early rebleed risk.
Thrombolysis is contraindicated in haemorrhage.
CT has already confirmed SAH.
Antiplatelets are not given in an acute bleed.

steps.x: E: Urgent referral to the regional neurosurgical centre. SAH: ABCDE then urgent neurosurgical referral.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man collapses with a sudden headache. In the emergency department his GCS is 7 (E1 V2 M4) and he is snoring with pooled secretions. His pulse rate is 54 bpm, BP 198/110 mmHg, respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. CT has not yet been performed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Secure the airway with endotracheal intubation
questions.e: ABCDE comes first: a GCS of 8 or less with airway compromise and hypoxia needs a definitive airway before CT and neurosurgical referral.

steps.x: Collapsed with reduced consciousness and an unprotected airway.

elim: BP control matters but the airway comes first.
Never before CT, and not before the airway is secured.
Given later once SAH is confirmed; he cannot swallow safely.
Imaging comes after the airway is secured.

steps.x: D: Secure the airway with endotracheal intubation. Airway first: GCS 8 or less = intubate.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman had a subarachnoid haemorrhage yesterday and her aneurysm was coiled this morning. She is alert with a GCS of 15. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. The team wants to reduce her risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia over the next 3 weeks.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medication?
questions.e: Oral nimodipine, started within 72 to 96 hours of the bleed, prevents vasospasm-induced cerebral ischaemia.

steps.x: After SAH; prevent delayed ischaemia.

elim: Antiplatelets do not prevent vasospasm and increase bleeding risk.
Steroids are not used in SAH.
Used short term for raised ICP, not vasospasm prevention.
A calcium channel blocker without the cerebral selectivity or evidence of nimodipine.

steps.x: E: Oral nimodipine. All SAH: oral nimodipine within 72 to 96 hours.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT angiography shows a wide-necked middle cerebral artery bifurcation aneurysm. The interventional neuroradiologist says the anatomy is unsuitable for endovascular treatment. He is alert with a GCS of 15 and his BP is 146/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
o: Conservative management with repeat CT angiography
questions.e: Endovascular coiling is generally preferred, but surgical clipping is the alternative when the aneurysm is unsuitable for coiling.

steps.x: The aneurysm must be secured but cannot be coiled.

elim: A ruptured aneurysm must be secured to prevent rebleed.
Usually preferred but unsuitable here.
Nimodipine is given for about 3 weeks and does not prevent rebleeding.
Treats hydrocephalus, not the aneurysm.

steps.x: D: Surgical clipping. Coiling first-choice; clipping if unsuitable.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has a subarachnoid haemorrhage from an anterior communicating artery aneurysm with a narrow neck. She has COPD and ischaemic heart disease. She is alert with a GCS of 15. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 150/90 mmHg. The neurovascular team meets to choose how to secure the aneurysm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: Endovascular coiling by an interventional neuroradiologist is generally preferred to clipping because it is less invasive with a shorter recovery.

steps.x: Suitable for coiling, poor surgical reserve.

elim: Treats carotid stenosis, not intracranial aneurysms.
For refractory raised ICP, not to secure an aneurysm.
Leaves a high risk of rebleeding.
An alternative, but more invasive with a longer recovery in a patient with poor reserve.

steps.x: C: Endovascular coiling. Secure the aneurysm: endovascular coiling preferred.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man taking warfarin for a mechanical aortic valve has a sudden severe headache. CT head confirms a subarachnoid haemorrhage and CT angiography shows a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. His GCS is 14, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg. Neurosurgery has accepted him for transfer.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management of his anticoagulation?
o: Continue warfarin because of the mechanical valve
Stop warfarin and give IV vitamin K 5 mg with prothrombin complex concentrate
Stop warfarin and give oral vitamin K 1 mg
questions.e: Warfarin with SAH: stop warfarin and give IV vitamin K 5 mg plus prothrombin complex concentrate for rapid reversal.

steps.x: Intracranial bleed on warfarin with a high INR.

elim: An active intracranial bleed takes priority; reversal is needed.
Reverses dabigatran, not warfarin.
Reverses heparin.
Too slow and too small a dose for an intracranial bleed.

steps.x: D: Stop warfarin and give IV vitamin K 5 mg with prothrombin complex concentrate. Warfarin + SAH: stop it, IV vitamin K 5 mg + PCC.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman is on day 3 after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. She has become increasingly drowsy and her GCS has fallen from 15 to 11 over 12 hours. She is not hyponatraemic. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 170/94 mmHg. CT head shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with no new blood.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF diversion
Start oral nimodipine at a higher dose
questions.e: Falling GCS with enlarged ventricles is hydrocephalus, from blood blocking CSF drainage; it needs neurosurgical CSF diversion (a drain or shunt).

steps.x: Falling GCS with large ventricles, no new blood.

elim: Her sodium is normal.
Contraindicated in haemorrhage and irrelevant to hydrocephalus.
Dangerous with raised ICP and possible obstruction.
Nimodipine prevents vasospasm, not hydrocephalus.

steps.x: D: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF diversion. Hydrocephalus after SAH: CSF drainage or shunting.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman telephones her GP surgery. Forty minutes ago she had a sudden explosive headache while running, which she describes as the worst she has ever had. She has vomited and feels drowsy. She has no history of headaches.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Advise paracetamol and review in 24 hours
Arrange an emergency ambulance to the emergency department
Book a routine GP appointment for tomorrow
Refer urgently to the neurology outpatient clinic
questions.e: A thunderclap headache is SAH until proven otherwise and needs emergency transfer for CT, with ABCDE assessment and neurosurgical referral if confirmed.

steps.x: Thunderclap headache with drowsiness in the community.

elim: Misses a potentially fatal bleed.
Far too slow for a thunderclap headache.
Still too slow; she needs same-day CT.
Not given before the diagnosis is confirmed.

steps.x: B: Arrange an emergency ambulance to the emergency department. Thunderclap headache: emergency admission for CT.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has bilateral flank masses and hypertension. Her mother had a subarachnoid haemorrhage at 45 and needed a kidney transplant. Genetic testing is offered. Her eGFR is 68 mL/min/1.73m² and urine dipstick shows blood +.
questions.q: Which is the most likely genetic cause of her condition?
o: PKHD1 mutation causing autosomal recessive disease
questions.e: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, most often a PKD1 mutation on chromosome 16, is associated with berry aneurysms and SAH.

steps.x: Familial polycystic kidneys with SAH in the family.

elim: Causes vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Causes Marfan syndrome.
Causes ARPKD, which presents in infancy.
Causes von Hippel-Lindau disease with renal cell carcinoma.

steps.x: C: PKD1 mutation on chromosome 16. ADPKD = PKD1, chromosome 16, a risk factor for SAH.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has an unruptured 5 mm aneurysm found incidentally at the junction of the anterior communicating and anterior cerebral arteries. He asks why the aneurysm formed in that place. He smokes and has hypertension. His BP is 154/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Tear in the tunica intima of the aorta
Weakness of the tunica media at an arterial bifurcation
questions.e: Berry aneurysms form at arterial bifurcations around the Circle of Willis due to congenital or acquired weakness in the vessel wall media.

clues: at the junction of the anterior communicating and anterior cerebral arteries
steps.x: A saccular aneurysm at a branch point.

elim: Causes thrombosis and ischaemic stroke, not saccular aneurysms.
Causes rare mycotic aneurysms, usually distal, from endocarditis.
Causes subdural haemorrhage.
Causes aortic dissection.

steps.x: E: Weakness of the tunica media at an arterial bifurcation. Berry aneurysm = media weakness at a bifurcation of the Circle of Willis.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman has a sudden severe headache followed by neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting. CT confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage. A student asks why the bleed causes such sudden pain and meningism. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 170/96 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: Arterial blood enters the CSF, suddenly raising ICP and irritating the meninges
Compression of the brainstem by a lens-shaped clot
Slow venous ooze stretching the dura
questions.e: Rupture releases arterial blood directly into the CSF-filled subarachnoid space, causing a sudden rise in ICP (thunderclap headache) and meningeal irritation (meningism).

steps.x: Explain the thunderclap and meningism.

elim: SAH is not an infection.
Describes an extradural haematoma.
Describes subdural haemorrhage, which causes gradual symptoms.
Vasospasm is delayed (7 to 14 days).

steps.x: A: Arterial blood enters the CSF, suddenly raising ICP and irritating the meninges. Blood in CSF: sudden ICP rise + meningeal irritation.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man is taking oral nimodipine after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. His aneurysm has not yet been secured because of a delay in transfer. He asks whether the nimodipine will stop the aneurysm bleeding again. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 144/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which statement about nimodipine is most accurate?
o: It dissolves the clot in the subarachnoid space
It lowers the risk of rebleeding by lowering BP
It reduces vasospasm and ischaemia but does not prevent rebleeding
questions.e: Nimodipine is a calcium channel blocker with relative selectivity for cerebral vessels; it reduces the severity of vasospasm and improves outcome but does not prevent aneurysm rebleeding.

steps.x: The patient confuses vasospasm prevention with rebleed prevention.

elim: It has no fibrinolytic effect.
It does not prevent rebleeding; only securing the aneurysm does.
It has no effect on CSF drainage.
That is vitamin K and PCC.

steps.x: D: It reduces vasospasm and ischaemia but does not prevent rebleeding. Nimodipine: less vasospasm, better outcome, no protection from rebleed.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man develops headache, vomiting and drowsiness 4 days after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT shows enlargement of all four ventricles with no obstructing mass. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt is planned. His pulse rate is 56 bpm and BP 174/96 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this complication?
o: Blood impairing CSF resorption at the arachnoid granulations
Excess CSF production by the choroid plexus
questions.e: Blood in the subarachnoid space blocks CSF resorption at the arachnoid granulations (communicating hydrocephalus) or causes obstruction, and may need shunting.

steps.x: All four ventricles enlarged: CSF is not being absorbed.

elim: Rare (choroid plexus papilloma), not the SAH mechanism.
Would cause swelling, not dilated ventricles.
CT shows no new blood.
Causes ischaemia at 7 to 14 days, not ventricular dilatation.

steps.x: A: Blood impairing CSF resorption at the arachnoid granulations. Hydrocephalus after SAH: blocked arachnoid granulations.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman develops hyponatraemia 4 days after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. She is euvolaemic, her urine is concentrated and her serum osmolality is low. Thyroid function and cortisol are normal. Her sodium is 125 mmol/L. A student asks why the bleed caused this.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Damage to the posterior pituitary stopping ADH release
Excess aldosterone from the stress response
Hypothalamic dysfunction causing inappropriate ADH release
questions.e: The bleed or raised ICP causes hypothalamic dysfunction with inappropriate ADH release, water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia (SIADH).

steps.x: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine after SAH.

elim: Her cortisol is normal.
Would cause diabetes insipidus with high sodium.
Would cause sodium retention and hypokalaemia.
Not the recognised mechanism.

steps.x: D: Hypothalamic dysfunction causing inappropriate ADH release. SAH causes SIADH via hypothalamic dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has a lumbar puncture 16 hours after a thunderclap headache. After centrifugation the CSF supernatant is yellow. A traumatic tap is unlikely because the red cell count does not fall between tubes. His GCS is 15 and BP 150/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the colour of the CSF?
o: Breakdown of red cells in the CSF to bilirubin
Fresh blood introduced by the needle
questions.e: Xanthochromia appears at least 12 hours after the bleed as red cells haemolyse and haemoglobin breaks down to bilirubin; the same breakdown products are thought to trigger delayed vasospasm.

steps.x: Yellow supernatant long after the bleed.

elim: Gives turbid, not yellow, CSF.
Fresh blood gives a clear supernatant after spinning.
Does not colour the CSF.
Does not give xanthochromia after a thunderclap headache.

steps.x: B: Breakdown of red cells in the CSF to bilirubin. Xanthochromia = haemolysed red cells and bilirubin, an older bleed.
